subject: MGMT464
title: Hurdle 9 · The Locked Gate — Leading Teams: Communication, Coaching, Conflict and Team Leadership

questions.stem: Identify the five steps of sending a message.
options: Develop rapport; state your objective; transmit the message; check understanding; get a commitment and follow up
Write the message carefully; send it; wait for a reply; remind the receiver; escalate to their manager if nothing happens within a day
State the message; repeat it in a louder voice; email it; text it; call to make sure it arrived
Plan what to say; organise the points; lead the conversation; control the reaction; review afterwards
questions.why: Sending a message is a skill with steps. See §9.1.

questions.stem: Describe how to check understanding.
options: Ask the receiver to paraphrase, or ask a question only someone who understood could answer — not 'is that clear?'
Say 'is that clear?' and accept the nod, because adults will always ask if they have not understood what was said
Send the message twice in two different media so that it cannot be missed
Wait for complaints, because a misunderstood message shows itself in the results

questions.stem: Identify the textbook's rule for choosing the medium.
options: The richer the message, the richer the medium — a hard message face to face, never by text
Always email, because a written record protects both the sender and the receiver if there is a dispute later
Always text, because short messages are read immediately and cannot be misunderstood
Always in writing, because spoken messages are forgotten within a day

questions.stem: Explain what went wrong with 'finish the analysis section' in question 1.
options: No objective, no specification, no check of understanding — step 4 would have exposed the gap in thirty seconds
The receiver was lazy and did not ask what the sender actually meant by 'the analysis section' before starting the work
The deadline was too short for the receiver to produce a complete analysis
The medium was wrong, because an instruction of that kind should have been written down

questions.stem: Identify the listening step most leaders fail first.
options: Do not interrupt
Take notes
Face the person
Ask open questions
questions.why: Most leaders fail at 'do not interrupt' first. See §9.2.

questions.stem: Describe feedback as the textbook defines it.
options: The process of verifying messages and determining whether objectives are being met
Criticism of a person's performance delivered by the manager at the annual review
An annual review in which the manager and the employee agree the rating for the year
A compliment given to an employee who has performed well in front of the team
questions.why: Feedback turns communication into results. See §9.2.

questions.stem: Identify why people do not give feedback to leaders.
options: They fear the reaction, were never asked, assume the leader knows, or saw what happened to the last person who spoke
They are shy by nature and do not like to speak in front of senior people, especially in a meeting with the whole team present
They are busy and feedback takes time away from the work
It is against policy in most organisations for staff to comment on their managers
questions.why: Why people do not give feedback. See §9.2.

questions.stem: Identify what a leader must do to get feedback.
options: Ask for it, thank the person who gives it, and act on it visibly
Wait for it, because people who have something to say will find a way to say it
Demand it, because feedback is part of every employee's job
Pay for it, because people give honest feedback only when there is something in it for them
questions.why: Psychological safety, one conversation at a time. See §9.2.

questions.stem: Identify the four steps of the coaching model.
options: Describe current performance; describe desired performance; get a commitment to the change; follow up
Blame the person; warn them formally; punish them if it continues; replace them if it still continues after that
Praise the person; pay them more; promote them; celebrate the promotion with the team
Plan the task; delegate it; measure the result; reward the person who delivered it

questions.stem: Describe how to state current performance.
options: Specific, observed, recent — behaviour, not character: 'the last three reports arrived after the deadline', not 'you are unreliable'
General and about character, so that the person understands the whole pattern of their behaviour over the year rather than one incident
Vague and old, so that the person is not embarrassed by a recent example
As a threat, so that the person understands the seriousness of the conversation

questions.stem: Explain why 'ask, do not tell' matters in step 3.
options: A commitment the person states is one they own
Asking is polite and keeps the relationship warm during a difficult conversation
Telling takes longer, because the person has to be convinced
Asking avoids paperwork, because the commitment does not have to be recorded

questions.stem: Identify the cost of silence about the under-performing team member in question 2.
options: The two people doing his work, the resentment they hide, and the member who never learns he has a problem
Nothing — silence is kind and protects the team's relationships, which matter more than one member's missing work
A fine from the university for failing to report the problem
A complaint to HR from the member who is not performing

questions.stem: Identify the five conflict-management styles.
options: Avoiding, accommodating, forcing, negotiating, collaborating
Fight, flight, freeze, fawn and flee
Decide, consult, facilitate, delegate and ignore the conflict
Win, lose, draw, quit and appeal

questions.stem: Describe the collaborating style.
options: High concern for own and others' needs — work jointly for a solution that satisfies both; the preferred style and the hardest
Give in to the other party to keep the peace, putting their needs above your own and hoping that the goodwill will be repaid later
Use authority or power to win the conflict regardless of the other party's needs
Split the difference so that each party gets part of what it wanted

questions.stem: Identify when forcing is appropriate.
options: An unpopular decision must be made fast, safety, or the other party is taking advantage — at a cost to the relationship
Always, because a leader who does not force the decision loses the respect of the team and the confidence of the organisation above
Never, because forcing destroys relationships and should be avoided at any cost
Only with friends, who will forgive the leader afterwards

questions.stem: Identify the three parts of a BCF statement.
options: Behaviour, Consequences, Feelings
Blame, Criticism, Fury
Boss, Colleague, Friend
Background, Context, Facts and Figures
questions.why: Plan a BCF statement that keeps ownership of the problem. See §9.4.

questions.stem: Describe the in-group and out-group in Leader–Member Exchange.
options: In-group: trusted members who get attention, information and opportunity; out-group: formal, transactional treatment
In-group: new staff who need the leader's attention; out-group: experienced staff who can safely be left alone to get on with the work
In-group: managers who report to the leader; out-group: workers who report to the managers
In-group: friends of the leader outside work; out-group: family members and relatives who work in the organisation

questions.stem: Identify how the two groups form.
options: Early and fast, from perceived similarity, competence, initiative and willingness to take extra roles
By lottery, because leaders cannot pay attention to everyone and so end up choosing more or less at random
By seniority, because the longest-serving members earn the leader's trust first
By salary, because the highest-paid members are the ones the leader consults
questions.why: How the two groups form. See §9.5.

questions.stem: Explain what the out-group's perception of favouritism does.
options: Equity theory says it destroys motivation for everyone who sees it
It motivates them to work harder so that they can join the in-group
Nothing — the out-group accepts that the leader has favourites
It improves cohesion, because the out-group forms its own team
questions.why: What high-quality exchange produces — and its cost. See §9.5.

questions.stem: Identify the leader's fix for in-groups.
options: Widen the circle deliberately — build high-quality exchanges with all members, not a chosen few
Abandon the trusted people so that the out-group does not feel excluded
Hide the in-group so that the out-group does not notice the favouritism
Pay the out-group more to compensate them for the attention and opportunity they do not receive

questions.stem: Identify what a leader should NOT delegate.
options: Personnel matters — appraisals, discipline, confidential issues; crises; activities specifically assigned to the leader
Paperwork and routine tasks that the leader has always done personally and knows how to do faster than anyone else in the team
Technical matters that others in the team can handle as well as the leader
Tasks with developmental potential that would stretch a follower

questions.stem: Identify the four steps of the delegation model.
options: Explain the need and why this person; set objectives defining responsibility, authority and deadline; develop a plan with the follower; establish checkpoints and hold accountable
Give the order; wait for the result; check the work when it arrives; blame the follower if it is wrong; do it yourself next time
Ask for a volunteer; hope someone takes it; forget about it; repeat the request when nothing happens
Email the task; remind the follower; escalate to their manager; redo the work yourself

questions.stem: Identify the three things that must travel together in delegation.
options: Responsibility, authority and accountability
Pay, title and office
Time, budget, staff, equipment and information
Vision, mission, values and strategy
questions.why: Dumping is responsibility without authority. See §9.6.

questions.stem: Identify why leaders do not delegate.
options: Fear it will be done worse, fear losing control or credit, belief it is faster themselves, lack of trust, never learned how
Delegation is illegal for certain tasks under employment law, so leaders keep everything themselves to be safe from the consequences
Followers refuse delegated tasks because they are not paid for them
Delegation costs money, because followers have to be trained first
questions.why: Every one is visible to the team. See §9.6.

questions.stem: Identify the seven characteristics of effective teams.
options: Norms, leadership, cohesiveness and interdependence, composition, structure, organisational support, creativity
Size, age, pay, office, hours, titles, laptops, parking spaces, the coffee machine and the view from the window
Vision, mission, values, slogan, logo, website and app
Trust, speed, cost, quality, risk, scope and time

questions.stem: Identify the three parts of conducting an effective meeting.
options: Planning, conducting, follow-up
Opening, middle and end
Agenda, lunch and close
Talk, vote and leave the room quickly

questions.stem: Describe when the leader should decide how the team decides.
options: Before the discussion, not after
After the vote, once the result is known
Never — the team should decide how it decides
During the argument, when it becomes clear that agreement is impossible

questions.stem: Identify the contents of a team charter.
options: Purpose; goals and success measures; roles; decision rule; meeting rhythm; norms for deadlines, attendance and disagreement; what happens when someone does not deliver
Names, phone numbers, email addresses and home addresses of every member of the team, together with their timetables, their preferred working hours and their photographs
The budget for the project and who is authorised to spend it
The leader's biography and the reasons they were chosen to lead the team

questions.stem: Describe a self-managed team.
options: A relatively autonomous team whose members share or rotate leadership and hold themselves mutually accountable
A team with no goals of its own that organises its work as it sees fit and reports to nobody at the end of the week
A team run by an appointed director who makes all the decisions
A team of one person who manages their own workload

questions.stem: Identify the work self-managed teams are best for.
options: Complex, knowledge-based work with experienced members
Routine, structured, time-critical work with clear procedures
Crises, where speed matters more than commitment
Simple repetitive tasks where little judgement is needed

questions.stem: Identify top management's role for self-managed teams.
options: Design for it — clear boundaries, resources, reward systems for team results, and a champion who protects the team while it learns
Leave the team entirely alone from the first day, because any involvement from above undermines its autonomy and teaches it to wait for instructions from the top
Appoint a strict leader to make sure the team does not drift
Cancel training, because self-managed teams learn by doing
questions.why: Challenges and top management's role. See §9.8.

questions.stem: Explain the chapter's reading of the 'polite' team in question 4.
options: Politeness is the symptom — missing norms about disagreement and accountability, no decision rule, and a conflict-avoiding leader
Politeness is the strength — the team has avoided the relationship conflict that destroys other teams and should be congratulated
The team is too small to disagree productively
The team needs a bonus to motivate members to speak

questions.stem: Exercise 1A: a manager emails 'Sort out the client complaint'; two days later the client has been called twice by two different people. Determine the missing skill and the steps skipped.
options: Sending a message — no objective, no check of understanding, no commitment (steps 2, 4 and 5)
Listening — the manager did not take notes of what the client said
Delegation — the manager gave responsibility without authority
Delegation — the manager gave responsibility for the complaint without the authority to settle it, so two people acted
questions.why: Answer key: A sending — steps 2, 4, 5. See §9.1 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Exercise 1B: a supervisor says in front of the ward, 'You are always late with the charts'; the nurse says nothing and is late again. Select the rewrite as the first two coaching steps.
options: 'The charts for beds 3–7 came in at 3 p.m. today and yesterday; I need them by 1 p.m. so the afternoon doctor has them.'
'You are unreliable and everyone on the ward knows it, so this is the last time I am going to say anything about the charts.'
'Try harder next week, because the doctors are starting to complain about the charts and I cannot keep covering for you.'
'Late again — I'm writing you up this time, and if it happens once more you will be moved to another ward.'
questions.why: Answer key: B — current then desired, behaviour not character, in private. See §9.3 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Exercise 1C: two engineers disagree about a design; the project lead says 'work it out between you' and leaves; a week later they are not speaking. Determine the style used and the style needed.
options: Avoiding; the situation needed collaborating with the lead facilitating
Forcing; the situation needed accommodating by one engineer so that the project could move on
Negotiating; the situation needed avoiding until tempers cooled
Collaborating; the situation needed forcing by the lead
questions.why: Answer key: C avoiding → collaborating. See §9.4 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Select the BCF statement one engineer in Exercise 1C could open with.
options: 'When the design changes without our agreeing, I have to redo the load calculations, and I feel my work is not respected.'
'You never listen to anyone and you are wrong about the design, as you have been wrong about every design before this one.'
'The lead should decide this, not us, because we clearly cannot agree on anything.'
'I give up — do what you want with the design and I will calculate whatever you send me.'
questions.why: Behaviour, consequences, feelings. See §9.4 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Exercise 1D: a department head consults the same two people on every decision; the other six have stopped offering ideas. Determine the pattern and the fix.
options: An LMX in-group — widen the circle deliberately
Delegation failure — the head should delegate more decisions
Meeting failure — the head should write an agenda
Coaching failure — the head should follow up with the six
questions.why: Answer key: D LMX in-group. See §9.5 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Exercise 1E: a ninety-minute meeting covers five topics, decides nothing and ends with 'let's think about it'. Determine what was missing.
options: Planning, a decision rule and follow-up — no agenda, no decision rule, no minutes
A bigger room with a better screen so that everyone in the department could see the slides and follow the discussion from the back
More participants so that every view was represented
A longer meeting so that every topic could be settled
questions.why: Answer key: E meetings. See §9.7 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Exercise 1F: a director does every appraisal herself, delegates none of the routine reports, and works until 9 p.m. Determine what she should delegate and what she should keep.
options: Delegate the routine reports; keep the appraisals
Delegate the appraisals; keep the reports because they are confidential
Delegate everything so that she can leave at 5 p.m.
Keep everything, because a director is accountable for all of it
questions.why: Answer key: F delegation. See §9.6 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Exercise 2A, the silent consultancy team: two dominate, three agree with everything, one stopped attending, a wrong assumption went unraised for a week; the leader is friendly, avoids conflict, has never written an agenda and grades everyone the same. Determine the missing characteristics, the conflict style and the LMX pattern.
options: Missing norms, structure (roles, decision rule) and leadership; the leader is avoiding; the in-group is the two dominant members
Missing composition only; the leader is forcing the group to agree with her; there is no in-group because everyone contributes equally to the work
Missing organisational support only; the leader is collaborating; everyone is in the in-group
Nothing missing; the leader is negotiating; there is no pattern
questions.why: Marking guide, task 1. See §9.7, §9.4, §9.5 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Exercise 2A: select the leader's first proper agenda for the next meeting.
options: Objectives, items with owners, a decision rule, and times — sent in writing before the meeting
'Catch-up — 2 p.m. in the usual room' sent by message on the morning of the meeting, with no items listed
A list of topics with no times or owners, so that the meeting stays flexible
No agenda; keep it informal so that members feel free to raise anything
questions.why: Marking guide, task 2. See §9.7 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Exercise 2A: select the four-step coaching conversation with the member who stopped attending.
options: Current: three absences; desired: attend and own one section; ask for a commitment rather than tell; set a follow-up date
'You're out of the team — we have carried you for long enough, the deadline is too close, and nobody has the time to chase you any more.'
'Everyone misses meetings sometimes — don't worry about it, we will catch you up.'
'Attend the next meeting or I'll report you to the module leader.'
questions.why: Marking guide, task 2. See §9.3 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Exercise 2B: your own team names one task to delegate 'with authority'. Determine what must travel with it.
options: Responsibility, authority and accountability — plus objectives, a deadline and checkpoints
Just the task itself and a reminder a day before the deadline so that it is not forgotten by the person who took it on
Only the responsibility, because authority stays with the leader
Only the credit, so that the person is motivated to deliver
questions.why: Step 2 prevents dumping. See §9.6 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Exercise 2B: each member writes one BCF statement about the team to say aloud. Select the correctly formed one.
options: 'When the slides arrive the night before (B), I rehearse at 1 a.m. (C), and I feel the deadline isn't shared (F).'
'You people are always late with everything, I am tired of it, and I am going to tell the module leader if it happens again.'
'The slides are a disaster and we are going to fail if this continues.'
'I'm fine with whatever the rest of you decide about the slides.'
questions.why: Marking guide, task 4. See §9.4 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Exercise 2B: the rewritten charter must include norms for disagreement and missed deadlines. Determine why those two norms matter most for the silent team.
options: Without them, politeness replaces challenge and non-delivery has no consequence — the exact failures in the case
They are required by the university's project guidelines and the module leader checks that they are in every team's charter
They are the shortest norms to write and agree
They replace the decision rule, which the team does not need
questions.why: Answer to question 4 and the charter. See §9.7.

questions.stem: Take-away: a team member is asked 'when did you last tell the boss something they did not want to hear?' and answers 'never — the last person who did was moved'. Determine the finding.
options: Feedback is not asked for, thanked or acted on — people have seen what happens to the last person who spoke
The boss is a great listener who has never needed correcting, which is why the team has nothing to add to his plans
The team has nothing to say because the boss is always right
Feedback is unnecessary in a well-run team

questions.stem: Take-away: the leader says 'I treat everyone equally'; a member says 'the interesting work always goes to the same three people'. Determine the reading.
options: An in-group the leader does not see — the gap between the two answers is the finding
The member is wrong, because the leader knows better than anyone how the work is allocated
The leader is lying, because leaders always have favourites
Nothing — both are right from their own point of view

questions.stem: Take-away: the minutes show every decision — even the lunch order — signed off by the leader. Determine what the team can decide without the leader.
options: Nothing — a conventional team, not a self-managed one
Everything, because the leader signs off what the team has already decided
Only hiring, because that is what leaders keep
Only methods, because the leader decides the goals

questions.stem: Rami shouts across the river 'do the thing we discussed!' and Dana does the wrong thing. Determine the sending steps missed.
options: State the objective, transmit specifically, check understanding
Develop rapport only — Rami should have asked how Dana was feeling first
Get a commitment only — Rami should have asked Dana to agree
Choose a written medium — Rami should have sent a note

questions.stem: Omar has dropped the rope three times this week. Rami says: 'You dropped the rope Monday, Wednesday and today; I need both hands on it until I say release — can you commit to that?' Classify the conversation.
options: The coaching model — current, desired, commitment asked
A BCF statement — describing behaviour, consequences and feelings
Forcing — Rami is using his authority
Delegation — Rami is handing Omar the rope

questions.stem: Noor and Dana argue about the camp site; Rami says 'we have time, and both of you matter — let's find a site that gives Noor the view and Dana the water'. Classify the style.
options: Collaborating
Forcing
Avoiding
Accommodating

questions.stem: The gang is minutes away; Rami overrides the discussion and orders everyone up the ridge. Determine the style and whether it fits.
options: Forcing — appropriate when safety demands a fast decision
Avoiding — inappropriate because the argument is unresolved
Accommodating — inappropriate because Rami gives in
Collaborating — ideal because everyone's needs are met
questions.why: Safety; an unpopular decision made fast. See §9.4.

questions.stem: Rami always consults Noor first and gives her the scouting; Omar and Dana notice and start holding back. Determine the pattern and the cost.
options: An LMX in-group — the out-group perceives favouritism and reduces effort
Delegation — Omar is lazy and uses Noor's favoured position as an excuse for holding back
Self-management — ideal because Noor leads herself
Coaching — fine because Noor is being developed

questions.stem: Rami tells Dana to arrange the horses but gives her no gold and no right to bargain; the villagers refuse her. Classify the failure.
options: Dumping — responsibility without authority
Over-delegation — Dana was given too much
Good delegation — Dana should have found a way
A coaching failure — Dana was not trained to bargain
questions.why: Responsibility, authority, accountability travel together. See §9.6.

questions.stem: At the locked gate all four must pull at once, on a signal, with each person on a named rope. Determine the team characteristics this demands.
options: Structure (clear roles) and interdependence — members need each other to succeed
Creativity only — the team must find a completely new way through the locked gate
Organisational support only — the team needs the village's help
Size only — four is the right number for the ropes
questions.why: The Locked Gate — roles and interdependence. See §9.7.

questions.stem: By the final day the four decide the route, rotate who leads each stretch and hold each other to the plan while Rami only facilitates. Classify the team.
options: A self-managed team — shared leadership, mutual accountability
A conventional team — Rami still facilitates and holds the authority
A crisis team — formed for the final day
An out-group — the four have excluded Rami
questions.why: When the team leads itself. See §9.8.

questions.stem: Rami starts each evening with three questions: what do we decide tonight, who owns it, and how do we decide — vote or consensus? Determine what he is doing right.
options: Planning the meeting and setting the decision rule before the discussion
Avoiding conflict by structuring the evening so tightly that nobody has the chance to disagree with him
Forming an in-group of those who own decisions
Dumping decisions on the followers

questions.stem: Identify the benefits of self-managed teams.
options: Higher productivity, quality and flexibility, faster response, higher commitment, lower turnover, and members developed as leaders
Lower cost only, because the team needs no manager and the salary saved can be spent on better equipment for the team to use in its work
Fewer meetings, because the team does not need to coordinate
Less training, because the team teaches itself

questions.stem: Rami gives the hardest news of the journey — that Omar's village has been raided — by sending a note with a runner. Determine the chapter's verdict on the medium.
options: Wrong — the richer the message, the richer the medium; a hard message is given face to face
Right — writing is a record that Omar can keep and reread
Right — runners are fast and Omar needs to know quickly
Wrong — it should have been sent through Noor, who knows Omar best and could soften the blow

questions.stem: Before giving Dana the river task, Rami asks about her brother and then says 'I need two things from you tonight'. Determine the steps shown.
options: Develop rapport, then state the objective
Transmit the message, then check understanding
Get a commitment, then follow up
Check understanding, then transmit the message

questions.stem: Noor tells Rami the plan is wrong; he thanks her in front of the team and changes it. Determine what this does for future feedback.
options: It makes feedback safe — ask, thank and act on it visibly
It weakens his authority in front of the team at a critical moment
It encourages rebellion against future plans
Nothing — Noor would have spoken anyway
questions.why: Why people do not give feedback — and what makes them. See §9.2.

questions.stem: Rami prepares his reply while Omar is still speaking, then interrupts him. Determine the listening steps broken.
options: Stay tuned in and do not interrupt
Take notes of what Omar is saying
Face the person who is speaking
Ask questions to clarify Omar's point

questions.stem: Determine the organisational form of feedback the chapter links to the project's peer evaluation.
options: 360-degree feedback — from manager, peers, subordinates and customers
Annual appraisal by the module leader
Exit interview at the end of the project
A customer survey of the organisation studied, collected by the project team at the end of the interview

questions.stem: After Omar commits to both hands on the rope, Rami forgets to watch at the next crossing. Determine the coaching step missed.
options: Follow up — set the date, check, recognise the change
Describe current performance — the three dropped ropes
Describe desired performance — both hands on the rope
Get a commitment — Omar's agreement

questions.stem: Omar, in the out-group, starts taking initiative, delivering early and supporting Rami's plan. Determine the chapter's advice he is following.
options: The follower's role — earn a high-quality exchange through initiative and delivery
Complain to the elders about Rami's favouritism and ask them to order the captain to treat every follower the same
Form his own in-group with Dana against Noor
Withdraw effort until Rami notices him
questions.why: The role of the follower. See §9.5.

questions.stem: Rami hands the gang-prisoner's questioning — a confidential, disciplinary matter — to Dana. Determine the chapter's verdict.
options: Wrong — personnel and confidential matters should not be delegated
Right — a leader should delegate everything that can be delegated
Right — it develops Dana's skills in a difficult area
Wrong — Dana is too junior for the task, but a more senior follower could have taken it on

questions.stem: The village guards start deciding their own rota and methods, but the elders give them no boundaries, no resources and no champion; conflict spreads. Determine what is missing.
options: Top management's design — clear boundaries, resources, team rewards and a champion
A stricter leader appointed by the elders to take back control of the rota and make the decisions the team cannot make for itself
Fewer guards so that the team is easier to manage
More rules so that the guards know exactly what to do
questions.why: Challenges and top management's role. See §9.8.

questions.stem: Determine the kind of work for which a conventional, leader-directed team remains best.
options: Routine, structured, time-critical work
Complex, knowledge-based work with experienced members
Creative work with experts who know the field
All work, because leaders are always needed
